headline: Families Displaced by the Ardillos Return Home in Guerrero, Mexico
article_body:
More than 15 families displaced by the Ardillos criminal group in Mexico returned to their homes in Guerrero, according to an August 16 statement by the Federal Ministry of the Interior (Secretariat de Gobernación – SEGOB).

In May, the Ardillos launched an offensive against rival criminal groups and local police forces in the rural, mountainous region known as Guerrero’s Montaña Baja. Mexico’s Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said the attacks were part of an attempt by the Ardillos to expand territorial control and push out a rival clan known as the Tlacos. The Ardillos reportedly used high-caliber weapons and explosive-laden drones in a wave of violence that lasted more than a week.

Their origins can be traced to factions associated with the Beltrán Leyva Organization and the Gulf Cartel, which once profited from heroin production and trafficking in Guerrero’s mountainous regions. However, following a series of arrests and deaths of their leaders during the 2010s, the organizations splintered into several groups, including the Ardillos and the Tlacos.

Since then, the Ardillos have consolidated their presence across several municipalities in the region, including Chilapa, Quechultenango, Mochitlán, Tixtla, Juan R. Escudero, Zitlala, Atlixtac, Ahuacotzingo, and Acatepec. It inherited part of the heroin trade and later diversified into illegal mining and the extortion of Indigenous communities.

Its ability to impose control over these territories rests in part on its capacity for violence. The Ardillos have access to sophisticated weaponry, including high-caliber firearms and explosives deployed using drones. This has spread fear among residents and fueled several waves of violence over the past two decades. In 2020, for example, communities in the area drew national attention after images emerged of young children taking up arms to protect themselves from Ardillos incursions.

But the group’s power also stems from its deep roots in local political structures. Bernardo Ortega Jiménez, for example, the brother of alleged Ardillos leader Celso Ortega Jiménez, has held several political positions in Guerrero, including serving as mayor of Quechultenango from 2002 to 2005 and two terms as a state legislator. In addition, Mercedes Carballo Chino, Celso Ortega Jiménez’s sister-in-law, is currently the mayor of Chilapa.

headline: The ‘Bukele Effect’ on Latin America’s Security
article_body:
Under President Nayib Bukele, El Salvador has become a popular exemplar for fighting organized crime in Latin America. And throughout Latin America and the Caribbean, leaders are attempting to follow the Bukele playbook. 

In a few short years, Bukele managed to overpower the country’s gangs, the Mara Salvatrucha (MS13) and Barrio 18. His success stems from near-complete control of the Salvadoran government, which allowed him to implement emergency powers suspending many constitutional rights. Salvadoran security forces have arrested tens of thousands of alleged gang members and pushed them into overcrowded prisons with severely restrictive conditions. Mass trials have handed down sentences amounting to thousands of years.

headline: Brazil’s Biggest Banking Fraud Scheme Explained
article_body:
Almost a year after an investigation into Brazil’s biggest-ever banking fraud scandal, authorities are only now beginning to understand the full extent of the money laundering, political corruption, and gang ties behind the alleged operation at Bank Master.

The case first broke in November 2025, when the Central Bank of Brazil (Banco Central do Brasil – BCB) liquidated Bank Master, citing evidence of serious financial regulatory violations. The BCB bypassed the traditional judicial process and immediately initiated an extrajudicial liquidation to repay creditors and prevent a bank run.

Days later, authorities arrested Bank Master’s owner, Daniel Vorcaro, in São Paulo’s Guarulhos Airport. The police believe he was trying to flee the country.

SEE ALSO: Murder at Brazil’s Busiest Airport Exposes Failures in Witness Protection

The investigation continues today, and on June 26, the BCB dismantled Sefer Investments, a financial institution accused of obscuring the funds diverted by Bank Master. Sefer Investments is now the third company liquidated as part of the scandal, aside from Bank Master itself.

How Did the Fraud Work?

Vorcaro presented himself as an ordinary, successful Brazilian entrepreneur, but authorities say that beneath that façade lurked a sophisticated criminal operator.

At the heart of Vorcaro’s alleged operation was a Ponzi-like scheme. Bank Master raised money by selling Bank Certificates of Deposit (Certificados de Depósitos Bancários – CDBs), or bank-issued fixed-income products. In simpler terms, investors lend money to a bank in exchange for an agreed interest rate. Bank Master promised a higher return than its competitors could afford to attract investors. The problem, according to authorities, was that Bank Master could not afford it either. 

After Bank Master was paid for the fraudulent CDBs, it invested the money in a credit fund where it was the only investor. Vorcaro allegedly diverted this money to companies linked to his family and partners. Part of the resources were also sent to shell companies and funds controlled by front men, according to investigators. This made it so Bank Master needed new investors to pay off the original investors, and then newer ones, and so on. It was unsustainable, and Bank Master did not have the liquid assets to pay back the loans.

Bank Master also allegedly sold fake or low-quality portfolios of payroll-backed loans—a type of credit that is paid back automatically from people’s salaries or pensions—promising other institutions a return they would not get. The bank offered loan portfolios to institutional investors, pension funds, retirement funds, and other banks. This was supposed to generate profit for the buyers, as they acquired the portfolios for a fixed price and would receive the equivalent value plus interest. However, the portfolios were fake or worth less than promised, and buyers never got the expected returns.

Investigators believe Vorcaro laundered the money from these scams through Bank Master by moving funds between accounts to hide their true origin and overvaluing assets to attract investors.

A Portrait of Brazil’s Corruption Machinery

Investigators believe Voraco was able to operate with impunity for years thanks to deeply entrenched corruption inside Brazil’s financial sector and government.

SEE ALSO: Historic PCC Bust Spurs Brazil Crackdown on Digital Money Laundering

According to Bruna Perez, an anti-money laundering consultant, Bank Master stands out from other financial scandals because the bank’s owner was using his own institution to launder money.

“If the bank is required by the regulator to have an anti-money laundering department to prevent money laundering, but the bank itself is laundering funds within its own system, how are you supposed to catch it?,” she told InSight Crime. “They were using the prevention apparatus to launder money.”

And while banks are expected to fight fraud internally, it is the government that sets and enforces the rules. So Vorcaro cozied up with top lawmakers and established links with politicians from left- and right-wing parties. Several senators have been investigated for taking bribes to pass legislation favorable to Bank Master, among them former President Jair Bolsonaro’s chief of staff, Ciro Nogueira, and Jaques Wagner, the former government leader in the Senate. 

Vorcaro is also accused of recruiting officials from financial institutions and security forces. In March 2026, he was charged with corrupting civil servants at the Central Bank, while several current and former police officers were also arrested for allegedly using confidential information to tip Vorcaro off about investigations and intimidating people that could expose his operations.

Vorcaro’s Criminal Iceberg

The complex web of actors and institutions involved in the Bank Master case also includes private militias and criminal organizations.

In addition to the financial crimes that led to his arrest, Vorcaro was charged with coordinating an armed enforcement wing dubbed “the Crew” (A Turma) to protect his criminal scheme.

In practice, the Federal Police (Polícia Federal – PF) described the Crew as a paramilitary structure led by Vorcaro that involved active and retired police officers, members of Rio de Janeiro’s militias, and operators involved in the illegal lottery known as Jogo do Bicho, or the “Animal Game.” One of Rio’s oldest criminal economies, Jogo do Bicho has grown incredibly popular, and today the criminal groups running these games are close with gangs, militias, and politicians.

SEE ALSO: Carnival, Samba, and Criminal Control in Rio de Janeiro

Armed with high-powered weapons and armored cars, the Crew allegedly threatened people who could disrupt Vorcaro’s businesses, surveilled targets, and illegally collected private information to threaten the lives and families of potential whistleblowers.

Vorcaro paid the gang at least R$ 400,000 (around $78,000) a month, according to the police. Investigators allege that a former car thief named Luiz Phillipi Machado de Moraes Mourão, alias “Sicário,” led the group, while a retired police officer named Marilson Roseno da Silva used his experience and contacts to surveil targets and collect sensitive information from police investigations and court proceedings.

The police investigation also uncovered links between the Crew and Brazil’s largest gang, the First Capital Command (Primeiro Comando da Capital – PCC). Reag Investments, one of the companies liquidated by the Central Bank for its alleged involvment in the fraudulent schemes, managed a fund suspected of receiving money from a fintech company operating for the PCC. Another company suspected of being run by a PCC member was hired to carry out a São Paulo city government project by the producer of former President Bolsonaro’s biographical movie, “Dark Horse,” which was partially funded by Vorcaro. The producer is under investigation for diverting funds from the project to the movie.

Voraco’s surveillance and intimidation operations also extended into the digital sphere. After Bank Master’s liquidation, Vorcaro signed contracts of up to R$2 million (around $390,000) with digital influencers to attack the Central Bank and promote Bank Master on social media, according to the Federal Police. The propaganda operation, called Project DV—Daniel Vorcaro’s initials—was also allegedly in charge of monitoring journalists and entrepreneurs seen as posing a threat to Vorcaro’s businesses.

headline: Ketamine Trafficking Expands Across Latin America
article_body:
More and more countries across Latin America and the Caribbean are reporting cases of ketamine trafficking, reflecting a shift in the region’s drug markets driven by the rise of synthetic drug cocktails and more dispersed supply chains.

On August 3, the Regional Prosecutor’s Office in Arica, Chile, convicted 17 alleged members of an organization that trafficked ketamine from Peru to Chile. Shipments crossed the Tacna-Arica border using drug couriers who entered the country on foot and were then flown on domestic flights to supply drug markets in the Metropolitan Region, according to the investigation.

A few weeks earlier, on July 13, the Arica Court upheld the convictions of 18 members of another group that smuggled ketamine between the two countries, which included Peruvian, Chilean, Venezuelan, and Ecuadorian nationals. According to local media, some of its members may have had ties to the Ecuadorian criminal group the Lobos, although authorities have not disclosed further details.

Both cases illustrate a growing regional trend. Used as an anesthetic in human and veterinary medicine, ketamine is increasingly circulating in illicit markets across Latin America and the Caribbean because of its growing use in synthetic drug mixtures, according to the latest World Drug Report from the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).

Although the Americas account for just 5% of global ketamine seizures, according to UNODC, the number of countries detecting the illicit trade in the substance has steadily increased, rising from none between 2006 and 2010 to 20 between 2021 and 2025.

The Rise of “Polysubstances”

For decades, ketamine occupied a marginal place in Latin America’s illicit drug markets. Although it has been used recreationally since it was first introduced as a pharmaceutical drug in the 1960s, its use was concentrated among small groups of consumers who gained access to it through contacts with medical supplies, with little involvement from organized crime.

But demand has surged alongside the growth of synthetic drug markets. The sale of mixtures containing multiple drugs, also known as polysubstances or “designer drugs,” has become increasingly common. These are substances with unique compositions designed to circumvent regulations and enhance the effects of traditional drugs.

In Latin America, this trend is reflected in the rise of so-called “tusi.” Although the name originally comes from the chemical compound 2C-B, today tusi rarely contains that substance. Instead, it is typically made from mixtures whose composition varies from one producer to another but which frequently include ketamine, MDMA, amphetamines, cocaine, caffeine, and medications such as paracetamol or acetaminophen.

SEE ALSO: Tusi: The Pink Drug Cocktail That Tricked Latin America

Ketamine also appears in other synthetic drug cocktails popular in the region, including some “speedballs”—mixtures of ketamine with stimulants such as MDMA—and the so-called “Calvin Klein” in Chile, a specific combination of cocaine and ketamine.

“Ketamine is a trendy drug and is highly sought after at electronic music parties. This has also helped it spread among an urban audience,” Pablo Zeballos, an organized crime researcher and former Chilean security official, told InSight Crime.

Chile, in fact, has emerged as one of the region’s largest consumer markets for ketamine, due in part to its relatively high levels of purchasing power per person and the prices synthetic drugs can command.

Low Barriers to Entry

Growing demand coincides with a key advantage for criminal networks: obtaining ketamine is often much easier than other drugs. Because it already exists as a widely marketed medication, traffickers do not need to manufacture the substance illicitly; they simply need to divert it from legal supply chains.

“We have detected several methods used to obtain [ketamine]: theft from veterinary facilities, recruiting people who work in the sale of the product, fraudulent purchases, forged prescriptions, diversion along the distribution chain, or illegal imports from neighboring countries,” Diego Chavarría, head of the Organized Crime Division of Costa Rica’s Judicial Investigation Agency, told InSight Crime.

Differences in regulations between countries facilitate this process, meaning trafficking occurs primarily between neighboring countries. Peru, for example, has fewer restrictions on the sale of ketamine than other South American countries, which has made it an important supply hub for Chile and Ecuador. In Central America, Nicaragua plays a similar role, according to Chavarría.

Once diverted from medical supplies, moving ketamine into the illicit market is also relatively straightforward. In liquid form, ketamine is transparent—earning it the nickname “water” in some countries—and can easily be concealed in ordinary containers. It can also be evaporated and crystallized into powder, which can then be transported in containers as small capsules.

In early July, for example, Chilean police dismantled a small laboratory in a residential area of Temuco, where liquid ketamine was being crystallized and divided into smaller quantities before distribution. Authorities seized more than 100,000 doses.

“Up to 40 doses can be obtained from one gram of ketamine, which is not common with other drugs,” Zeballos explained.

Transportation methods also rely on existing commercial infrastructure. Larger shipments, in the hundreds of kilograms or liters, are frequently moved overland in cargo trucks and private vehicles or by sea aboard fishing vessels traveling along the coast. Smaller quantities, from grams to tens of kilograms, are transported by drug couriers, often on commercial flights.

Authorities at Cancún International Airport in Mexico seized 2.6 kilograms of crystallized ketamine trafficked in carry-on luggage on a flight from Bogotá, Colombia. Source: Mexico’s Security Cabinet.

More recently, ketamine shipments from South America to Europe have also been identified, as demand there has likewise surged, according to the European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA). In March the Chilean Navy seized nearly 69 metric tons of drugs, including cocaine and ketamine—without specifying the amount of each—concealed in shipments of wood and rubber at the port of Arica bound for Germany and Italy.

“The could be that the logistics infrastructure built for cocaine trafficking to Europe is now being used for [ketamine], which offers high profit margins but faces less regulation and less police scrutiny,” Zeballos said.

A Highly Fragmented Supply Chain

No single criminal group controls the ketamine supply chain, or even specific parts of it. Low barriers to entry allow a wide range of actors to get involved, from large criminal organizations to independent networks and small-scale traffickers with no previous experience in drug trafficking.

“For now, the ketamine market appears to operate under conditions of polyarchy … different criminal organizations function as complementary links in the chain rather than as competitors,” Zeballos said.

The networks moving ketamine across borders are often multinational, as illustrated by the case of the group recently convicted in Chile. Another example emerged in Argentina in late 2025, where authorities dismantled a network of Paraguayan, Chilean, and Argentine nationals trafficking ketamine among the three countries.

Some larger criminal organizations have also established themselves along specific routes. Chilean prosecutors, for example, have identified the Colombian criminal group Los Costeños as a wholesale supplier of the substance along maritime routes between Colombia and Chile via Peru.

During InSight Crime field research in different parts of Chile, we found that the Tren de Aragua was one of the main drivers of the ketamine market, controlling trafficking from neighboring countries where it also had a presence and exploiting migrant communities as drug couriers.

At the local level, the networks that obtain ketamine or handle its retail distribution operate according to the criminal dynamics of each market. In Medellín, Colombia, for example—one of the region’s main hubs for tusi distribution—the drug mixtures are produced by individuals or small groups, but their sale is often overseen by larger gangs, including those linked to La Oficina de Envigado.

In Costa Rica, Chavarría explained, the procurement and distribution of ketamine is handled mainly by gangs dedicated exclusively to retail drug sales, with little involvement from criminal groups linked to the international trafficking of other drugs.

headline: Podcast | Gio and Fito: When Gangsta Rap Gets Real

Jorge Mora Villamar, known to his fans as Gio, was a rapper, music producer, and DJ. His talent lifted him out of poverty and off the streets of Guayaquil. But it also led him into the inner circle of Ecuador’s most notorious crime boss—and gave him a front-row seat to the criminal violence that has reshaped the country. 

When we met Gio in 2024, he explained the inner workings of the Choneros mafia and how they combined gang warfare on the streets with a “digital war” waged through their own stable of musicians. He also described the mafia maneuvers, alliances, and betrayals that had tipped Ecuador over into a period of relentless and brutal violence, which continues today. What Gio told us helped us analyze the structure of Ecuadorian organized crime and explain how a country once known as one of the most peaceful in South America could become one of the most violent places in the world.

The Choneros

The Choneros are criminal pioneers that have reshaped Ecuador’s underworld. Starting out as a gang of common street thugs, the group underwent a dramatic evolution while behind bars. Under the charismatic leadership of Jorge Luis Zambrano, alias “Rasquiña,” they recruited bands of petty criminals and youths into a criminal federation that took over the prison system and expanded around the country. The Choneros then used their power and reach to establish themselves as a mercenary army, hiring themselves out to transnational drug traffickers and criminal elites.  

The Choneros federation began to fall apart after the murder of Rasquiña in 2020, and the organization’s battles with splinter groups such as the Lobos, the Tiguerones, and the Chone Killers led to a series of brutal prison massacres. The national murder rate spiraled. Rasquiña’s successor, Jose Adolfo Macías Villamar, alias “Fito,” would become the face of this security crisis as he directed the Choneros from a prison that he had converted into his command center.

Fito escaped from prison in 2024 after Ecuador’s new hardline president, Daniel Noboa, ordered his transfer to a maximum security cell. But he was captured a year later and has since been extradited to the United States. The Choneros, meanwhile, have been in decline, losing power and territory as Ecuador’s ever more violent underworld undergoes a period of criminal fragmentation in which street gangs no longer respond to their mafia paymasters.

headline: The InSight Take: The Shield of the Americas Grows, But Does it Have a Strategy?
article_body:
Colombia just became the 19th member of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition—better known as Shield of the Americas—days after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew to Panama to declare its new motto: “We do bad things to bad people.”

On this week’s InSight Take, Managing Editor Deborah Bonello and Co-director Jeremy McDermott unpack what this fast-growing coalition actually commits its members to, five months after its founding and still without an approved operational plan. With lethal strikes on Caribbean and Pacific boats having killed over 200 people—and no evidence the US drug flow has slowed—they ask whether Shield of the Americas can actually disrupt organized crime.

Transcript

Deborah: [00:00:00] Colombia just became the 19th member of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, better known by its public-facing name, Shield of the Americas. We saw Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fly to Panama to make the announcement personally, and he told assembled ministers and chiefs of defense from across the hemisphere that the coalition’s new motto is “We do bad things to bad people.” He also used the platform to push member states to abandon the International Criminal Court.

Deborah: [00:00:31] So five months after Donald Trump signed the founding proclamation at his Doral resort in March, the coalition has grown from 17 countries to 19 and absorbed a new hardline Colombian government and sits along a parallel campaign, of course, of lethal strikes on boats in the Caribbean and Pacific that has killed over 200 people. We have no evidence that this campaign has interrupted the flow of drugs to the United States. Indeed, the wholesale price of cocaine in the US seems to be at an all-time low. But there have been some shifts in the modus operandi of drug smuggling.

Deborah: [00:01:08] I’m Deborah Bonello, managing editor of InSight Crime, and this week I’m joined by our co-director, Jeremy McDermott, to try to untangle what this coalition actually is, what it commits its members to. And perhaps the biggest question is what it’s actually capable of achieving. Jerry, thanks for joining me.

SEE ALSO: Timeline of US Strikes Against Alleged Drug Boats

Jeremy: [00:01:27] Good to be here. Good to talk about something which is essentially going to shape security policy for the next couple of years in the region. Deb.

What is the Shield of the Americas?

Deborah: [00:01:36] I think you’re right. And I think the best place to start, because I think there could be some confusion with our viewers who hear “Shield of the Americas” and “A3C” and aren’t sure if those two things are the same thing or two different initiatives. What can you tell us about that?

Jeremy: [00:01:56] They are the same thing. Two different names for it. The formal name, the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, came a wee bit later on. The initial use was of the “Shield of the Americas” branding that came out of that founding summit you mentioned in Florida in March, and the two names now seem to be interchangeable.

Jeremy: [00:02:22] Perhaps what’s interesting to focus on is not necessarily the name but how it came about. Before the announcement at the Doral summit, we had Hegseth, we had Stephen Miller, and the Southcom commander, General Francis Donovan, meeting with regional defense ministers in Miami and laying out some sort of groundwork. On March 7, President Trump signed the proclamation in which the Secretary of War established the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition as a military alliance that the White House says is built around a policy to use lethal force against cartel and narco-terrorist networks. That’s the founding document. And it’s worth saying, Deb, that since President Trump took office the second time, he’s put a list of criminal groups on the terrorist list. And, you know, I suspect this isn’t a coincidence. I suspect this is to enable the US to target these different criminal syndicates with less legal risk around it. So now we’ve got 19 countries signed up, with Colombia just literally signing up with the election of President Abelardo de la Espriella, who’s just taken office a bit earlier this month.

Colombia Joins the Shield of the Americas

Deborah: [00:04:00] Yeah. And Colombia joining does feel like something of a big deal because we were seeing a world where Colombia wasn’t at the table, Mexico wasn’t at the table, Brazil wasn’t at the table. So I guess this feels like kind of a positive thing for the coalition, because obviously the former president, Gustavo Petro, himself a former guerrilla, I believe, was not included in the founding meeting. What do you make of Colombia saddling up?

And this is where we’re waiting in a sense for the rubber to hit the road, in terms of operational scope, defined strategy, and therefore the aims of this coalition. Specific aims in terms of the new sheriff in town, which is how Hegseth and the US are now describing themselves. When I look at the signatories, they are, without exception, nations that are aligned politically with Washington. So there’s a lot of political rhetoric around this. There is, up until now, very little action. And there’s still not any definition of what all these different nations are going to do apart from work together and what the specific targets are, except drug trafficking and narco-terrorism.

Meanwhile, we’re seeing the missile strikes in the Caribbean, which have been going on for the best part of a year now. I believe they started in early September, and increasing talk from the Trump administration in terms of taking that campaign to land. We’ve seen those conversations taking place over the last week. How can it not have an approved plan by now? I mean, is that unusual?

Jeremy: [00:08:23] Yes, Deb, I think that’s a good word. Let’s look at other US initiatives. Let’s look at Plan Colombia, you know, perhaps the most ambitious US strategy against drug trafficking, which went into effect in the year 2000 in Colombia and had enormous impact. Then, you know well, the initiatives in Mexico and Central America that were very well-thought-out strategies that involved a wide portfolio of tools, not just the military. And they weren’t signed and announced until actually a strategy was in place and often had a document or manifesto attached to them. We haven’t seen this with the Shield of the Americas. So, you know, you and I are going to be largely restricted to a bit of speculation on this front. So let’s, let’s do some speculation.

Deborah: [00:09:30] Well, a little. And what Mérida had, and I’m sure the Colombia agreements too, amongst other things, were some very distinct human rights sort of safety catches in terms of, you know, the way that organized crime and drug trafficking was being attacked. And that brings me to the whole International Criminal Court element of this, which is, again, as much political as it is strategic because Hegseth did layer in that to membership. That he wanted to increase pressure on those companies to essentially abandon the ICC.

SEE ALSO: GameChangers 2025| How the Trump Administration Reset the Fight Against Organized Crime

Jeremy: [00:10:10] Yeah. This has got lots of moving parts, so let’s try and unpack some of it. This is obviously more about Washington’s agenda than tackling criminal threats in the region. And yet, as you correctly say, it’s packaged together as part of this Shield of the Americas, and allies are being encouraged to speak out against the ICC, and this is not to do with Latin America. It’s not even to do with the boat strikes, although that is the ostensible reason that the ICC may come for the different members. This is linked to Gaza and Afghanistan and various other things in the Middle East and other parts of the world. So Washington is trying to bundle quite a sensitive geopolitical issue into this alliance. And if it becomes an actual condition of being a member of this, then that changes the dynamic for the signatories, because it forces them essentially to take a position against international law as we know it. And many of these nations are, of course, already signed up to the ICC. So it’s a huge diplomatic issue. And what are they going to get in return for this?

Jeremy: [00:11:41] Now, at InSight Crime, we are not interested in politics except insofar as they affect policy and strategy against what we study, which is transnational organized crime. The issue of respect for human rights, which used to lie at the heart of US strategy and US aid, has now, of course, slipped very far down the list of priorities and perhaps even disappeared from view. It seems now when I bring this up, not for some liberal perspective, but because our research tells us that governments and security forces need to win over local communities if they’re going to have any chance of really tackling organized crime at its root, because where organized crime works in tandem with the civilian population, it becomes extraordinarily difficult to tackle on any level. And killing people without trial or killing people who you don’t even know who they are, in the case of the go-fast boats, suspending civil liberties, not following international law and due process. These all challenge the legitimacy of the rule of law and therefore state authority and over time, can undermine public support. And so, I worry about, and I’ll return to this, I suspect, in our conversations, short-term tactical gain or victory compared to long-term strategic legitimacy and success. And I feel that you’re going to sacrifice a lot by adopting just this side, the tactical side, in the long-term overarching chances of success.

What is the True Potential of Shield of the Americas?

Deborah: [00:13:34] Yeah. And as you said earlier, it’s hard to speculate on what the coalition is going to achieve given that we don’t really know what it’s setting itself up for exactly yet. But does it have the potential? You know, it’s not new to have regional states agreeing to collaborate with the US. We have seen this on and off for the last 50 years, perhaps not at such a sweeping regional level as we’re seeing now. But, you know, calling on what we already know about other anti-transnational organized crime efforts in the region. What does this new push have the potential to deliver?

SEE ALSO: GameChangers 2025 | US Reignites the War on Drugs and Weakens It for 2026

Jeremy: [00:14:19] I really think we need to be careful that I don’t think this is anything new. I think the rhetoric is new. But the United States has spent the last how many decades persuading, cajoling, and occasionally bullying nations in the region to cooperate with the US and, in many cases, each other in the fight against transnational organized crime. So, you know, this has been the centerpiece of US diplomacy and effort in our region. So let’s not paint this as something “wow” and something completely unprecedented. And we are absolutely in favor of regional cooperation to tackle transnational organized crime. It’s the only way to deal with transnational organized crime. So the idea that these nations pool intelligence, better coordinate training, and cooperate on stemming illegal financial flows, work together in denying safe havens to transnational organized crime networks that don’t recognize borders and move wherever the resistance is lowest. If the Shield of America actually does this and does this better in a well-thought-out and integrated way, then I think this is a good thing. I think it could lead to some real results. So let’s not see this as something completely new. The exclusively military rhetoric and perhaps the submersion of human rights as an element of US strategy and leadership. That’s the really new stuff.

Deborah: [00:16:13] Yeah, I agree there is some repackaging going on here to present this as something of a new idea. And like we say, it’s, it’s far from it. I suppose what’s different to the Mérida Initiative we saw in Mexico, for example, is that this is purely military. And in part that’s to do with the dismantling of USAID and basically the sort of softening of soft power in a sense, which has all but disappeared really from the US’s approach to organized crime here, but have we seen a purely military approach achieve success in the fight against drug trafficking and transnational organized crime?

Jeremy: [00:16:55] I’m going to go back again to tactical success and strategic. But listen, security force pressure is a really important element to any counternarcotics and anti-crime strategy. But in isolation, it’s not been proven to work in the long term. Let’s look at what has worked—what we’ve got concrete examples of.

SEE ALSO: Peace Never Had a Chance: Colombia’s ELN in Venezuela

Jeremy: [00:17:20] Colombia is probably the most concrete example. And when I arrived in the country in 1997, Deb, you know, there was a real threat of Colombia becoming a narco state. The Marxist guerrillas were camped outside and even within the three biggest cities, Bogotá, Medellín, and Cali. The Colombian state could not pretend to claim that it was governing more than half of the national territory. But then US aid in the form of Plan Colombia really was crucial in leading to a weakening of the illegal actors and the demobilization of two of the most powerful drug trafficking organizations, I would say in the world, certainly in the region, which were the United Self-Defense Forces of Colombia, a right-wing paramilitary organization, the AUC. It demobilized more than 30,000 people in this process. And then, the infamous FARC, or Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, a Marxist rebel group: they demobilized 13,000.

Jeremy: [00:18:33] Now, I think it’s hard to understate the importance of these two demobilizations in terms of transnational organized crime, in terms of drug trafficking, and in terms of Colombia’s national security and indeed the security of regions, because many of these groups had a presence outside of the country. But this was not achieved purely through military operations. That was certainly an important part of the equation. But economic and social investment, long-drawn-out negotiations, and political concessions were what carried this over the line. And USAID, which you mentioned, played a significant role in this process. And it was one of the more powerful pieces in the US toolbox to fight transnational organized crime. It’s gone. And the Shield of America seems to be suggesting that it can get things done through purely military tactics and strategy, and history in the region suggests that this is a flawed analysis.

SEE ALSO: Ecuador Criminal Profile

Deborah: [00:19:44] Okay, so let’s take the example of President Daniel Noboa in Ecuador as someone that has embraced both the political and security messaging from President Trump and is a very close ally to Washington. And he has employed a very militarized approach himself, placing gangs on his own terrorism lists and using economic tariffs against other nations. And now there are joint operations with the US on Ecuadorian soil. You know, we’re now two years into this. And what would you say, as an experienced observer of drug wars, have been the results of this approach in Ecuador so far?

Can Military Responses Alone Defeat Organized Crime?

Jeremy: [00:20:28] Yeah. President Noboa’s been the most enthusiastic and earliest recruit to President Trump’s rhetoric and tactics. And you mentioned one of the first things he did upon taking office was to declare the country’s gangs terrorist organizations and to declare an internal armed conflict, which allowed him to deploy the military to take the lead on national security, domestic security issues. And there have been some successes in killing and capturing, you know, the leaders of these groups.

Jeremy: [00:21:02] We know that the so-called kingpin strategy, which is, you know, taking out the leadership, has had mixed results. And in many cases, it’s actually led to more violence and more crime, not less. Yes, there are joint operations with the US forces. There’s intelligence sharing. There’s coordinated maritime operations. Yet so far, our fieldwork in Ecuador over the last two to three years hasn’t found any evidence of a significant reduction in the flow of cocaine through the country. The criminal groups have adapted to security force operations. They’ve become more clandestine, more sophisticated. And one thing that is beyond any doubt is that the level of homicides has reached record levels under President Noboa, and Ecuador’s moved from being one of the safer countries in the region just seven years ago to one of the most dangerous today. Homicide rates have jumped from just over seven per 100,000 in 2020 to 50 per 100,000 last year. So the country hasn’t become safer by unleashing the military. And in fact, it’s become really exponentially more dangerous to live in.

SEE ALSO: Durán: A Window into Ecuador’s Organized Crime Explosion

Deborah: [00:22:30] Okay. So with that in mind, as we look forward to the potential of this new coalition and its impact, its capacity to really impact transnational organized crime and drug trafficking. Is there a version of this that produces measurable results in that—without an architecture that mostly produces a rising body count—and has potential perhaps to produce more diplomatic wins than anything else? How do you see it?

Jeremy: [00:23:08] Let’s be glass half full about this. And let’s look at the more positive potential. I think there is a chance of short-term impact depending on where the resources are directed and whether or not they’re deployed in a systematic and constant manner over a longer period of time. What we’ve seen with the targeting of the go-fast boats, Deb, is it has changed modus operandi. Surprise, surprise, drug traffickers don’t want to use go-fasts as much. So, you know, it has had an effect on routes and on the vehicles or vessels that move drugs. What are going to be the results of this being taken on land and being adopted by all the nations that have signed up to Shield of the Americas, assuming that their constitutions allow them to deploy with the US, which I think people haven’t really been talking about. It’s not like the president can just turn around and go, “Sure, American troops just come in and fill your boots. No. The Constitution in many countries prevents foreign nations and foreign troops operating on their soil without the approval of Congress, and perhaps even Constitutional Courts. So let’s not get lost in the weeds. We’re a glass half full. So if this is applied in a strategic and constant way, it may well change criminal dynamics.

The Adaptability of Organized Crime

Jeremy: [00:24:50] One thing we’ve learned, Deb, in all of these years of looking at transnational organized crime is that it’s the most agile business in the world. It quickly adjusts to changing conditions. And if it has any infrastructure or leadership that is vulnerable to military strikes or operations, then it’s going to move to lower the risk by becoming more clandestine, hiding among the civil population, or maybe going like in the case of Mexico and the Jalisco cartel, which armed up its cartel, issued body armor, armored vehicles, point fives, and in certain, you know, scenarios took on the security forces head-on. So if we’re talking about, again, military action in isolation, there may be some tactical victories. It may force change to criminal dynamics.

SEE ALSO: Mexico Criminal Profile

Jeremy: [00:25:50] But this isn’t really going to have any long-term effect unless the planners are thinking about what to do next. Knowing that organized crime is going to adapt, they need to be playing 3D chess, and they need to be thinking, you know, how are they going to react? And we’re going to anticipate this by doing X and Y. The problem is the military toolbox is very limited. And if they hide in the civilian population, if they don’t present any targets for the military, then the military becomes a blunt and maybe even counterproductive tool in this fight, and we’ll see organized crime deepen its ties with local communities, broaden forms of criminal governance, and it may be that this particular cure worsens the disease rather than moves the dial in a long-term and strategic way to help Latin America contain and hopefully begin to dismantle transnational organized crime and drug trafficking.

Deborah: [00:27:07] Yeah. I mean, this feels like a good place to leave it. We could talk about this forever. We didn’t either sort of go into the issue of how criminal organizations are embracing cybercrime. They’re embracing crypto and so much…

Jeremy: [00:27:24] Drone warfare.

Deborah: [00:27:26] Yeah. So much technical innovation is happening within those criminal organizations, which governments are already behind on. So I think the devil really is going to be in the detail of the strategy of how they’re going to move forward in the coming months and years as to whether it’s going to produce any evidence that it’s working. And, of course, we’ll be watching pretty closely for that strategic document, or that strategic clarity, if it comes right. Jerry.

Jeremy: [00:27:57] Oh, yeah, we will pick it apart, assuming there is something to pick apart.

Deborah: [00:28:03] Well, thanks very much for joining me. And to you watching the Insight Take. Thanks for tuning in to our weekly video chat analysis on what are the biggest crime stories in Latin America. You can find it on our website, in the multimedia section, as well as on YouTube and Spotify. If there’s a story or subject you’d like us to take apart, please do reach out to me at flagship@InSight Crime.org and we’ll be back with another Insight Take next week. Bye for now.

headline: Reshuffled or Reformed? Venezuela’s Criminal Order After Maduro
article_body:
The arrest of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife on January 3 was an unprecedented aggression by the United States.  

At the time, President Donald Trump called Maduro the “kingpin of a vast criminal network”—the Cartel of the Suns—and linked him to Tren de Aragua and the Sinaloa Cartel, which his government has labeled terrorist organizations. 

This post is part of our annual Summer InSights series. See the full series here.

Maduro ran what we call “a hybrid state,” in which governance and crime became indistinguishable. Criminal groups became armed proxies for the state, crushing opposition and enforcing control in exchange for impunity. Corruption buried into state institutions—often mischaracterized as the Cartel of the Suns—used government as a private revenue generator.

Is gang violence spreading from Ecuador’s coasts into the capital?

1. Bomb Attributed to the ELN Wounds 14 in Cúcuta, Colombia

A truck loaded with explosives detonated outside a police command post in Cúcuta, Colombia, on the Venezuelan border, wounding 11 police officers and three civilians, according to Colombian authorities, who attributed the attack to an urban front of the National Liberation Army (Ejército de Liberación Nacional – ELN). The bombing coincided with near-simultaneous attacks on a police commander’s convoy and a congressman’s home in the same region, authorities reported. Authorities also foiled another attack in Cali, allegedly planned by the Central General Staff (Estado Mayor Central – EMC).

The attacks come just days before the August 7 swearing-in of Abelardo de la Espriella as Colombia’s president. The president-elect has vowed to break with predecessor Gustavo Petro’s approach of negotiating peace with the country’s criminal groups. Instead, de la Espriella gave armed groups an ultimatum: they had one month—ending when he takes office—to surrender or face the full force of the military.

2. Ecuador Deploys 4,000 Security Forces to Quito

Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa announced the deployment of 4,000 additional police and military personnel to Quito, days after police found a decapitated body hanging from a bridge there—a gruesome display more commonly associated with the country’s most violent cities, Durán and Guayaquil.

The move suggests the extreme violence long concentrated on Ecuador’s coast may be creeping into the capital, potentially a sign of gangs pushing into new territory as they fight for control of trafficking routes. During his tenure, Noboa has taken a hardline approach to combatting Ecuador’s criminal groups, with limited success.

3. Five Amazon Countries Wrap Up Environmental Crime Blitz

Authorities from Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru concluded Operation Green Shield 2026, deploying more than 3,600 officers to combat various environmental crimes across the Amazon basin between July 15 and 31. The operation, coordinated from Bogotá, led to 839 arrests and the seizure of 280,000 cubic meters of illegally logged timber, 195 metric tons of minerals and mining equipment, and thousands of trafficked animals.

Criminal networks are key drivers of environmental destruction in Latin America and the Caribbean, cashing in on global demand for gold, timber, and land. Green Shield shows what coordinated enforcement can achieve, though the criminal economies it targets remain deeply entrenched.

headline: The InSight Take: Abelardo de la Espriella Inherits Colombia’s Fractured Criminal Landscape
article_body:
Colombia’s new president faces one of the most complicated criminal landscapes in the world. In this week’s InSight Take, Co-Director Jeremy McDermott and Senior Colombia Analyst Sara Garcia unpack what Abelardo de la Espriella inherits: powerful armed groups like the Gaitanistas and the ELN, record cocaine production, and booming illegal gold mining. They weigh Washington’s likely support, whether de la Espriella can match the Uribe-era security gains, and the human rights risks of a harder military push.

Jerry: [00:00:00] Hello and welcome to another Insight Take. I’m Jeremy McDermott, co-founder and co-director of InSight Crime. And joining me is Sara Garcia, one of our senior Colombia analysts. Hi, Sara. How are you?

Sara: [00:00:13] Hi, Jerry. Thank you for having me.

Jerry: [00:00:17] Good to have you. And we’re going to talk about Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office on August 7th. He was elected, above all, on his promise to tackle the security situation, which has been worsening over the last few years. He inherits a really complex criminal landscape that’s actually been changing. We used to look at Colombia’s security situation through the optic of the civil conflict, which began in the 1960s here, which pitted Marxist rebels against right-wing paramilitaries. And then we had the US-backed government seeking to impose some sort of order on the country.

Jerry: [00:01:07] De la Espriella doesn’t recognize that Colombia is in a civil conflict.  For him, it’s the government pitted against a series of criminal actors. No ideology, no politics involved. As well as the criminal actors, Colombia is looking at booming criminal economies, led particularly by the cocaine trade, which we’re going to deep dive into in a wee bit later in the program. So let’s start by looking at these criminal factions and their relative strengths. So can you run through them briefly? Starting in order of importance?

SEE ALSO: Colombia Criminal Profile

Sara: [00:01:49] Sure. Well, first we have the Gaitanistas, also known as the Gulf clan. That remains the most powerful criminal organization in Colombia, with an estimated 10,000 members. The group controls much of the country’s northern region, particularly the Caribbean departments, and it’s continued to expand to the Pacific coast and also the Venezuelan border.

Sara: [00:02:15] Second, we have the National Liberation Army, or the Ejército de Liberación Nacional (ELN), which is the country’s second most powerful armed group with an estimated 7000 members alone. The traditional stronghold of the ELN is the Colombian-Venezuelan border, the more than 2000 km of the Venezuelan border, and it also extends into Venezuelan territory.

Sara: [00:02:47] And lastly, we have the dissident groups of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia, FARC, that, although there are several dissident groups, the two largest alone account for more than 7000 members.

SEE ALSO: Gaitanist Self-Defense Forces of Colombia (AGC) Criminal Profile

Jerry: [00:03:07] Right. So. Dummy’s guide to this, so that myself and all our audience are clear. In the North, we have the Gaitanistas in a kind of U along the Caribbean coast on the Panamanian border and beginning to push down either side along the Venezuelan border, and along the Pacific coast. We have the ELN concentrated largely along the Venezuelan border, although they do have some fronts in some of the center parts of Colombia. And then in the South, we have the FARC dissidents who are in a kind of a U along the bottom Pacific coast border with Ecuador, Amazonian region, up to Venezuela.

Jerry: [00:03:52] Okay. So. Many of these groups and the AUC or the paramilitaries that led to the Gaitanistas go all the way back to the Medellin cartel. The ELN have been around since the 1960s. The FARC dissidents can trace their roots back to the FARC in the 1960s. So a lot of these groups have got a long pedigree. Sara. So why are we talking about the current landscape being different?

Sara: [00:04:24] Yes. Well, the first element is the fragmentation of the criminal landscape. As you just mentioned, the AUC, or the Autodefensas Unidas de Colombia, the paramilitary blocks of the United Self-Defense Forces of Colombia. And they signed a peace agreement with the government in 2006. And only after that, 30 factions emerge from that demobilization alone. The Gaitanistas are one of the groups that emerged from that demobilization, but not the only one. And just ten years from that, in 2016 – 2017, another fragmentation process began amid the peace accords with the FARC. Various dissident groups emerged and are now fighting each other as much as any other criminal rivals in the country.

SEE ALSO: National Liberation Army (ELN) Criminal Profile

Sara: [00:05:21] Another element that is interesting in the current scenario is that little ideology remains. Most illegal armed groups operating in Colombia today are primarily motivated by economical gain and territorial control, and they are seeking to dominate strategic areas linked to illicit economies such as drug trafficking and illegal mining. These groups are able to tap into a wide portfolio of criminal economies, obviously led by the cocaine trade. Colombia has never in its history produced as much cocaine as it is producing today. But to that, you can add the growing marijuana business, illegal gold mining, environmental crime, extortion, and kidnapping, and you have billions of dollars in earnings every year. And this is allowing the different groups to increase not only in size but also in territorial reach and also in sophistication. The use of drones and other emerging technologies has transformed the dynamics of the country, and that’s enabling criminal groups to innovate more rapidly and in several areas, stay one step ahead of the authorities.

Jerry: [00:06:40] Yeah, I still believe that the ELN cling to some ideology. Although I think many of their fronts or units on the ground may not so much. But if there’s any one of the players for me that’s still ideological. I think it would, it would be the ELN. But you broke down some of the criminal economies. Let’s focus for a second on cocaine. It’s probably the most lucrative, and it’s certainly what Colombia is most famous for, unfortunately. And as you said, Colombia’s producing more cocaine than ever before. The numbers are a little hazy because last year’s figures were not published because President Gustavo Petro, the previous president, didn’t want these numbers out there because he thought it’d make him look bad. And indeed, we’re pretty certain that it would have done. But what we are pretty certain of is that Colombia is producing more than 3000 tons of cocaine a year.

Jerry: [00:07:44] So we’ve got an enormous increase in supply. We’ve got this fragmented landscape that you’ve been talking about. I think it’s worth talking about the markets as well, because there’s been some massive changes there. Historically, cocaine went to the United States and it went to Western Europe. That is no longer the case, particularly now with such a huge supply, those two markets simply can’t absorb that amount of cocaine. And that’s one of the reasons we’ve seen huge drops in prices over recent years in the US and in Europe. Drug traffickers have been diversifying their markets in an aggressive strategy. Australia is perhaps the most notorious, one of the places where cocaine wholesale reaches its highest price, but also we’re seeing multi-ton seizures in Asia.

Jerry: [00:08:48] So there is a concerted effort to use all this extra supply to diversify the consumer markets. And the Colombians can’t do this on their own. And what they have done, to be honest right from the beginning, is partner up with other mafias. First of all, it was the Mexican mafias, the Guadalajara cartel, and then they became Sinaloa, you know, and that was for the US market. The Colombians and the Mexicans partnered up for that. Then we saw the Colombians moving drugs into Spain themselves. But then later they developed quite a close relationship, and it was actually the AUC who did this with Colombia’s Ndrangheta, now arguably the most powerful of the Italian mafias, thanks to the cocaine connect. But now we’re seeing all sorts of diverse actors, mainly Europeans, in the cocaine business.

Jerry: [00:09:47] We’ve got the Dutch, we’ve got French traffickers, British traffickers, Albanians, and other Balkan mafias. Even Scandinavian criminals have been caught over here in Colombia. And this has changed the nature of the cocaine trade because no one group, thanks to the fragmentation in Colombia, really controls national supply or even a significant percentage of national cocaine supply. So the Europeans are able to make deals with smaller Colombian groups. And the Colombians, of course, want the profit margin that comes from selling cocaine wholesale, be it in the US, be it in Europe, be it in Australia, rather than selling it for $2,000, which is the average price of a kilo of cocaine in Colombia. But what’s interesting is that cocaine actually does have a rival in terms of criminal earnings in Colombia, doesn’t it? And this is the gold trade. What can you tell us about it?

Sara: [00:10:55] Yes. Illegal gold mining has become a key element of the criminal activities of illegal armed groups in Colombia. And this particularly has to do with the surge in international gold prices, which has fueled the expansion of both legal and illegal mining across the country. Another factor that is making gold particularly attractive is that illegally extracted gold can be laundered and incorporated into the legal supply chains, whereas cocaine remains illicit throughout every stage of the production and distribution. And what’s currently happening is that the illegal armed groups are capitalizing on the boom of of illegal and legal mining, and they are extorting legal and illegal miners in gold-producing regions, gaining multi-million dollar revenues through extortion alone. And when you combine those profits from extortion with the profits they gain from the direct involvement in illegal mining, the scale of these illicit revenues becomes even more significant.

Jerry: [00:12:12] Yeah. And as you say, if you’re caught with a kilo of gold, no crime for the most part. You’re caught with a kilo of cocaine, which is worth less now than a kilo of gold. And you know, it’s straight to prison. So gold is the ideal criminal economy and criminal commodity because it’s very easy to legalize, as you say. Prices are very high, but also they can use it for money laundering and to move large amounts of wealth across borders, leaving absolutely no trace. And they can use it to pay off their subcontractors. Again, leaving no trace. So gold, I think, is hugely important now for every major criminal group in Colombia for all of these different reasons. So we’ve looked at criminal groups; we’ve looked at criminal economies. That’s a quick overview of the panorama that de la Espriella is facing. What’s he promised in terms of policies or strategy to tackle these different complex threats?

Sara: [00:13:28] Well, during his presidential campaign, he stated that if elected, his administration will adopt a hardline security strategy, ruling out peace negotiations with illegal armed groups in favor of law enforcement and military approaches. And he actually also emphasized this in his inauguration speech on August 7th, in which he stated that he will seek to defeat the narco-terrorists, combat all criminal organizations, and that the only option available to illegal groups was to surrender or to face the force of the state. He also proposed resuming aerial eradication of illicit crops, coca crops using drones and bioherbicides. Although implementing such a policy will entail significant logistical, financial, and legal challenges for de la Espriella. 

Sara: [00:14:29] It is important to note that most of these proposals are not new in Colombia. Similar security and counter-narcotics strategies have shaped the government policy for several decades now. But, however, criminal organizations have demonstrated a strong capacity to adapt, while illegal economies have remained resilient and even in some cases, continue to expand.

Jerry: [00:15:00] Yeah. His campaign and his inaugural speech very much seemed to come out of the Washington playbook. President Trump threw his support behind de la Espriella, and is promising to step up aid, but we’ll come on to that in a sec. But this military first, this hard line, this mano dura approach we’re seeing increasingly in different parts of Latin America. President Noboa in Ecuador has been at it for now almost three years. President Kast in Chile, obviously we’ve got President Bukele in El Salvador, President Milei in Argentina. De la Espriella, if you like, is the last or the latest example of this move to the right and hardline security echoing much of the messaging coming out from the Trump administration. Colombia, of course, has been Washington’s most loyal ally for decades, although the last four years under President Gustavo Petro, a former guerrilla, were the exception that proved the rule. And Petro and President Trump ended up doing a lot of fighting over social media as well as on diplomatic forums. But can you just go back to Washington’s traditional role in Colombia? And then we’ll throw it forward and see what might change with the Trump / de la Espriella relationship.

And one of the defining moments in that relationship was the Plan Colombia, a multibillion-dollar initiative that was launched in the 2000s. The Plan Colombia was initially conceived as a strategy to combat drug trafficking organizations, and reduce coca production. But in the context of armed conflict in Colombia, it quickly evolved into a broader security partnership between the two countries. Much of the assistance provided by the US focused on strengthening Colombia’s security forces through training, military equipment, intelligence capabilities, and also counternarcotics programs. And the reality is that the results were mixed because US assistance contributed to a major transformation on Colombian security institutions and helped the government weaken several major armed factors. But while coca cultivation declined at certain points, production shifted geographically, and criminal organizations adapted to those changing conditions. So the strategy was effective at targeting the leadership and military capabilities of armed groups. I think it was successful, quite markedly successful. And people forget that it was US aid that really tipped the balance for the Colombian state and, I feel, forced the AUC and the FARC to negotiate. So from that perspective, I think there is some success to the US aid on that front. But let’s talk about US aid now.
