De la Espriella really needs to use this 100 days to move the dial in some way, and I’m worried that he won’t be able to start the coca eradication as quickly as he wants because of constitutional and environmental issues, that he’s not going to have any money to unleash the military in the way that he’s been discussing. And there’s also this emphasis on military action, which, of course, at InSight Crime we think is really only one part of a much wider toolbox that is needed to contain transnational organized crime and then begin to dismantle it. But, based on the last 30 years of experience and based on what de la Espriella has promised, what is your reading of how efficient and how effective his security policy could be?

Sara: [00:22:36] Well. To give the current scenario the benefit of the doubt, there is a clear trend toward a territorialization of Colombia’s criminal dynamics. So the violence is increasingly concentrated in specific areas that are strategic for criminal economies, particularly drug trafficking and illegal mining. And in this scenario, that territorial concentration could present an opportunity for Abelardo de la Espriella. Actually, several experts I have interviewed are that security policies should be far more targeted, grounded in a detailed understanding of local conditions, and tailored to the specific dynamics of the territories that are most affected by violence and also criminal governance. So in that case, that territorialization may help him.

Sara: [00:23:37] And the same logic applies to coca cultivation. Although coca is grown across several regions in the country, the vast majority of cultivation is concentrated in just ten municipalities. So this geographic concentration could make it easier to design and implement interventions focused on areas where they are likely to have the greatest impact. However, as I mentioned earlier, these measures have really already been used in the past, and drug trafficking has continued to grow, as has organized crime. So as you mentioned, the toolbox has to be more comprehensive than just the military approach or the counter-narcotics approach.

Jerry: [00:24:24] Yes. I’m going to reveal my age now. I remember going down to Putumayo, which is one of the main coca-growing regions in the late 90s, just as Plan Colombia was being designed and then implemented in 2000. We’ve been here before, Sara. And yes, I agree that if he’s able to do a very quick and very extensive coca eradication program within the ten municipalities that you mentioned, he could certainly make a dent in production. But we’ve seen what happened before when this was attempted with the aerial spraying; the crops just spread around Colombia. The fields got much smaller, so they didn’t provide a target for the aircraft. The yield per hectare went up. So on its own it might have a short-term effect, but organized crime has already adjusted to this once before and will do so again, I suspect with even greater agility and speed than than it did before.

SEE ALSO: Timeline of US Strikes Against Alleged Drug Boats

Jerry: [00:25:40] President Petro, the previous president, had kind of an interesting approach to drug policy. He switched from concentrating on the eradication of drug crops to seizures and trying to target the higher links in the cocaine trade. His argument, which was a powerful one, was, why are we punishing the poor cocoa farmers who make the least money in all of this, and are often simply victims of civil conflict and violence? Why don’t we concentrate on the upper links in the chain? Makes sense. He wasn’t able to execute this, and he wasn’t able to contain coca growth and cocaine production. So. What do we think is going to change with De la Espriella? And do we think that he really can, in the four years of his term, change the dynamics of the cocaine trade?

Sara: [00:26:59] Well, you mentioned Petro’s approach, and it was certainly an interesting idea. And I do think that it was important to open the discussion about which measures can effectively target those upper links in the drug trafficking chain, where the majority of profits are being made. And as you also mentioned, unfortunately, the implementation of that drug policy faced significant challenges, particularly due to the lack of coordination with other security policies and the total peace, and also for the international context and the struggles between the relationship with the United States. Well, de la Espriella has stated, as I mentioned earlier, through his campaign and reiterated in his inaugural speech that he will resume aerial eradication of coca crops. Okay. That’s something that has been made in the past, but history has shown us that these measures alone are insufficient. Focusing only on coca crops in certain regions can lead to a balloon effect that you mentioned earlier. And that may lead to an increase of cultivation in other parts of the country. And again, the coca crops are only one part in the drug trafficking chain. And it’s not the part that generates the highest profits for the whole transnational cocaine trafficking.

Sara: [00:28:49] We have seen in the past in different countries across the region that more effective approaches include comprehensive strategies, for example, including international cooperation, intelligence sharing, and judicial collaboration, dismantling of money laundering networks, following the money, following the brokers, among other measures.

SEE ALSO: Can A New President’s Hard-Line Approach Stop the Spread of Coca in Colombia?

Jerry: [00:29:19] Ironically, I think the United States had the right approach in previous administrations, where they balanced the security and hardline aspects with supporting the judiciary with obviously training, but also via USAID, engaging with local communities in the violent areas involved in the coca trade. And people don’t really give them the credit that is due. This actually had a very significant effect. And I believe that one of the reasons that coca is concentrated just in ten municipalities now, where the Colombian government doesn’t have much control, is because in other parts of the region there was systematic engagement. There was the arrival of all the organs of the state, not just police and army, but education and health and everything else. That, for many areas, was the first time they’d actually seen all of the presence of the state.

Jerry: [00:30:33] So anyway, we’ve been concentrating on the countryside. We talk about coca crops, the rural actors, and mining. But this isn’t just about the countryside. The cities are also suffering high levels of violence in some cases, and have their own criminal dynamics that President de la Espriella is going to have to deal with. Tell us a little bit about that.

Sara: [00:30:57] Yeah. Actually the urban conflict is one of the more underappreciated parts of the picture in Colombia, because even if the armed conflict remains concentrated in rural areas, we’ve seen that criminal dynamics are increasingly affecting Colombia’s major cities, for example, through extortion, homicide rates, robbery, and criminal intimidation, and that has been contributing to the growing perception of insecurity in the cities. In the cities, we have seen the presence of smaller criminal networks, but also the cities have become increasingly important for larger criminal networks because they concentrate strategic assets, for example, drug trafficking; they concentrate the ports, the transport infrastructure, financial services, and they concentrate consumer markets. And the reality is that criminal organizations are investing more in urban operations not only to generate revenue, but also to secure logistics, recruit members, launder money, which means that the reality today is that we can’t understand the security challenges that the country is facing if we don’t include in that understanding the dynamics of the urban areas.

SEE ALSO: The InSight Take: Colombia Turns Right With Abelardo de la Espriella. Here Are the Washington and Security Challenges.

Jerry: [00:32:30] What we’ve learned also over the last 30 years is that Colombia’s criminal groups are extremely agile, and they’re not going to take this new hardline policy lying down. There’s so much money at stake that we’ve discussed. Many of the groups have so much military experience. Think of the ELN that’s been resisting US-backed military offensives for decades now. What’s your thought on the adaptability of criminal groups to resist the switch in policy?

Sara: [00:33:10] Without a doubt. Colombian criminal groups have decades of experience in how to confront governments, how to push their own agendas and interests through violence, and also how to respond to these military approaches that de La Espriella is hoping to implement. If we have in mind, only this weekend, the weekend of the presidential inauguration alone, there were about 12 armed attacks in different parts of the country, mostly committed by the ELN, but also by FARC dissidents. And I do think that the message behind this may be that the groups are showing their operational capacity and signaling their operational capacity, but also their willingness, and sending the message to the government that they are willing to maintain the pressure on the pressure through violence, on civil society, on communities, but also on the armed forces.

Jerry: [00:34:22] The last president who used a lot of this, this hard-line dialogue, was President Alvaro Uribe. He was president from 2002 for two terms, two four-year terms. What we saw there, unfortunately, was the unleashing of the military also led to some systematic abuses of human rights, and the Colombian military doesn’t have the greatest human rights record. And much of Colombia’s civil conflict going back to six decades is linked to abuses by the state and the lack of political opportunities, political violence, etc. tell us a little bit about this dark history and whether there’s a risk of history repeating itself.

Sara: [00:35:12] Well, as you say, unfortunately, we will need much more time to fully discuss Colombia’s long history of state abuses. Under the previous governments, the country witnessed the consequences of stigmatizing social protest, the emergence of false positives that were these perverse incentives that led the military to murder civilians and falsely present them as members of illegal armed groups in order to claim operational rewards. We have seen the collaboration between the state actors and paramilitary groups, the persecution, and the extermination of political movements. So yeah, we definitely have a long story of state abuses. And unfortunately, this legacy continues to shape Colombia’s political landscape. The risk has not disappeared. We had the assassination of a presidential hopeful last year. Some of the underlying conditions that contributed to these abuses, such as the weak state present in certain territories, the institutional vulnerabilities, the polarization, the use of violence as a political tool. Well, those are elements that remain unresolved in the current scenario.

Jerry: [00:36:37] When I look back at President Uribe and his democratic security policy and then President Santos, who came after him, their great success wasn’t just the hard-line military and security force operations. It was that, in tandem with negotiations, President Uribe managed to demobilize the paramilitaries; 30,000 of them handed over weapons. President Santos managed to demobilize the FARC. 13,000 guerrillas. De La Espriella has refused to countenance any kind of negotiation. And my feeling is he’s slightly shot himself in the foot, because what, if anything, Colombian history shows us with the fragmentation that you’ve talked about is so long as the criminal economies remain intact on the ground, somebody’s going to manage them. And you’ve got to negotiate with the big groups, and then you’ve got to replace their presence and develop the legal economy. So, I want to be optimistic. Sara, I really wish President de la Espriella the greatest success in the world in reducing violence and tackling some of the immensely complex criminal threats that he’s facing. But we know there’s no silver bullet. We know that the criminal economies and revenues seem to be going up, not going down. 

SEE ALSO: Peace Never Had a Chance: Colombia’s ELN in Venezuela

Jerry: [00:38:25] Anyway, Sara, I’m sure after the first 100 days of this administration, we will sit down again, and we will have a chat about the success or not of this current Colombian strategy of President de la Espriella.

Jerry: [00:38:43] Thanks a lot for joining me for this fascinating chat. Thank you, our audience, for joining us. If you want to go deeper on any of these issues that we’ve been discussing, the ELN, the Gaitanistas, the history, it’s all on our website. Please go to InSightCrime.org, browse at your leisure. There’s all sorts of goodies there for you to read.

Jerry: [00:39:09] You’ve watched the Insight Take, a weekly video chat analysis of the biggest crime stories in Latin America and the Caribbean. You can find the links to this on our website in the multimedia section or on YouTube and Spotify. If there’s a story you want us to talk about that we haven’t already tackled, please send us a message at flagship@insightcrime.org, and we’ll see if we can put something together for you. We’ll be back next week with another insight take. Bye for now.

headline: Podcast | Three Ways to Lose a Son
article_body:
A mother searches for three missing children amid the wreckage of decades of armed conflict in Buenaventura, Colombia.

*This episode is also available in Spanish.

Listen on

YouTube
Spotify
Amazon
Apple

About This Episode

Buenaventura is Colombia’s main Pacific port and one of the continent’s most strategic corridors for cocaine trafficking. For decades, the city has been a battleground between guerrilla groups, paramilitaries, and criminal gangs fighting for control of drug routes toward Europe and North America. The result is a city where men and women are killed, children disappear, and families learn to live with grief and uncertainty as a permanent companion.

In this episode, we travel to Buenaventura and meet Elena, an Afro-Colombian woman in her sixties who arrived in the city as a child after armed groups killed her parents in her hometown. Buenaventura took her in, and she made it her own. She had seven children and built a life.

But the war that brought her there never left. Three of her children have disappeared.  Two vanished without a trace, leaving Elena searching in vain for clues to their fate. The skull of the third was found in an estuary three years after he disappeared.  

Through Elena’s story, we investigate how the armed conflict in Buenaventura has corroded the social fabric of the city. And we explore how violence does not just kill—it erases people, breaks families apart, and leaves mothers waiting for answers that sometimes arrive too late and sometimes never arrive at all.

Transcription

[00:00:01] Steven Dudley: Hi. This is Steven Dudley, co-director of InSight Crime. Just one thing before we get started. We’ve changed the names of all the people involved in this story to protect their identities.

Okay. Here’s the story. It’s Saturday morning. Our investigators Henry Shuldiner y Juliana Manjarrés are sitting in a hotel conference room in Buenaventura Colombia’s Pacific Coast.

[00:00:29] Elena: Bien, gracias a Dios, el Señor me lo bendiga.

[00:00:32] Steven Dudley: Across the table from them is a woman in her 60s. Afro-Colombian. Braids. She’s short but sturdy. We’re going to call her Elena.

[00:00:40] Elena: Estaba durísimo.

[00:00:43] Henry: Estaba duro.

[00:00:43] Elena: Y cuando llueve…

[00:00:47] Steven Dudley: She doesn’t raise her voice – she doesn’t have to. In Buenaventura, people listen. She’s been in the middle of this country’s civil war for decades.

[00:00:55] Henry: Tenemos un mapa porque estamos muy mal ubicados.

[00:00:58] Henry: We came to talk to Elena about how Buenaventura changed in that time period. From a city where kids played in the rain into a war zone where kids disappeared. 

Elena knows every little corner of the area, so I told her I was a little lost and put a map I was carrying in front of her.

[00:01:15] Elena: Yo te ubico por aquí. Esta es la isla. ¿Te vienes por aquí? Por aquí. Por aquí. Dónde está.

[00:01:21] Henry: Buenaventura snakes from the mainland to an island in front of a large bay, where the city’s port is. There’s a bridge that connects the two. Most people live on the mainland, but the fight over the strategic corridor and launchpad for drugs stretches across both of these areas and beyond.

[00:01:41] Elena: En esta parte se empieza en la isla y se termina.

[00:01:45] Henry: Sí.

[00:01:46] Elena: Hacia arriba.

[00:01:47] Henry: In Buenaventura, the lines on a map don’t just mark neighborhoods. They mark territory. Held by guerillas. By paramilitaries. By Street Gangs.

[00:01:59] Steven Dudley: Elena has lived through every wave of that violence in the worst way. Over the years, three of Elena’s children have gone missing, or “disappeared”< as they like to say. Three. And she’s not stopped looking for any of them. Welcome to InSight Crime’s Podcast where we take you behind the headlines to the frontlines of organized crime in the Americas. I’m your host, Steven Dudley, InSight Crime’s co-director.

[00:02:39] Henry: And I’m Henry Shuldiner. In this episode, I’m going to tell you the story of a mother in Buenaventura looking for her three sons in the middle of a brutal war over a strategic cocaine corridor.

[00:02:39] Henry: Three searches. And three very different outcomes. Elena wasn’t born in Buenaventura. But she’ll tell you she’s from there.

[00:03:08] Elena: Soy una hija de Buenaventura.

[00:03:10] Henry: I’m a daughter of Buenaventura, she likes to say. From the beginning, her life has been shaped by war. She arrived as a small girl from the heart of the coffee growing region in central Colombia, after armed groups killed her parents. She doesn’t remember much or doesn’t want to talk about it, about either the armed groups or her parents. What she remembers is what came after. A happy childhood. Hide-and-seek in the streets. And the rain.

[00:03:39] Elena: Una alegría era un aguacero en Buenaventura.

[00:03:43] Henry: It would come down in buckets she told us. But for Elena it was a joy. One of her favorite things to do was frolic in the puddles accumulating outside. The rain also fostered food, in abundance, which Elena said people readily shared.

[00:03:58] Elena: Los pescadores traían plátano, banano, papa, china, coco…

[00:04:06] Henry: The boats would pull up next to the houses, she told us. Plantains. Bananas. Yuca. Coconuts. The neighbors shared everything – this for so-and-so, this for so-and-so. That was Buenaventura, she said. 

Elena eventually trained as a nursing assistant and became a mother at a young age. She had seven children – five boys, two girls. 

But things were tough. She split with her partner. Some of the kids went to live with him, some with her. By then, around the mid-1990s, things were also changing in the city.

[00:04:40] Elena: Entonces yo diría que alrededor del 95, 96 empezaron aquí las masacres.

[00:04:47] Henry: Bodies started popping up in the river – tied to logs, floating north with the current. They were victims of massacres, the first of their kind in the area. 

But they were emblematic of things to come. The fight was between right-wing paramilitaries and left-wing guerrillas. Buenaventura is Colombia’s only Pacific port. It’s also right next to the country’s biggest coca growing region and the FARC – then-Colombia’s largest insurgency – was getting deeper into cocaine trafficking. 

They wanted the port. So, they came for it. 

The battle soon came to the city. Elena remembers the first time the FARC launched a full-scale attack on Buenaventura. It was 1997.

[00:05:35] Elena: La noche fueron disparos, fueron ráfagas. Fue una noche verdaderamente de terror.

[00:05:43] Henry: Gunshots and machine-gun fire all night, she said. Two young men from her block were shot. She drove them to the hospital. But they died. 

For a while this pattern continued. Fighting. Injuries. And Elena tending to them all. After all, that’s what she trained for. Until they came for her.

[00:06:05] Elena: Me amenazaron con revólver en mano. en la cabeza, me pusieron el revólver.

[00:06:11] Henry: She didn’t give many details but said that someone put a gun to her head and told her to stop helping people.

[00:06:17] Elena: Me ha tocado ver caer muchos, muchos, muchos, muchos, muchos.

[00:06:24] Henry: A lot of people. A lot, a lot, a lot. And that, she says, is when fear really took hold in the port.

[00:06:30] Elena: Y entonces empezó realmente la zozobra.

[00:06:40] Henry: People left, especially young people, who didn’t see a future, and who didn’t want to get caught in the fray. Others disappeared. One of those young people was one of Elena’s sons. We’re going to call him Luis. 

Luis was about ten years old when a man came around saying he was taking some kids to a bike race. Luis went and he didn’t come back. Helena had no idea what happened. She searched everywhere. And when she didn’t find him, she went to the local radio station which gave airtime for people to send messages to their missing relatives and loved ones. 

Still, in her heart, she knew he might have been kidnapped or worse. But she kept looking.

[00:07:29] Elena: Me contaban los compañeritos que era que el señor era ecuatoriano y que andaba robándose a los niños para que robaran para él.

[00:07:36] Henry: Other kids in the neighborhood told her the man was Ecuadorian, and that he was stealing children to make them steal for him. Her heart sank. Luis was gone. Elena lost her second son just a few years later. Esteban, as we are calling him, was her youngest. The apple of her eye. The tallest of her boys, dark-skinned like her, with tightly curled hair.

[00:08:07] Elena: Si todos mis hijos son guapos, pero él, sobresalía.

[00:08:12] Henry: All my kids are handsome, she told us, but he stood out.

[00:08:14] Elena: Ese jugaba fútbol y eso mantenía con una tula para arriba y para abajo.

[00:08:19] Henry: Esteban was also restless, energetic. He wanted to be a soccer player–and wore shorts and a jersey all the time. He lived with his dad, his stepmother, his grandmother and a few siblings. But Elena saw him a lot.

[00:08:33] Elena: Entonces ya no vivía ahí en la casa. Pero yo, frecuentemente iba.

[00:08:40] Henry: When Esteban was a teenager, he’d spend his days with friends in the woods or on a muddy field the boys carved out for themselves to kick the ball around. But something was off.

[00:08:50] Elena: La abuelita de él me comentó que no, que estaba muy rebelde.

[00:08:56] Elena: His grandmother told Elena that Esteban had become rebellious. And that the stepmother was blaming Esteban for everything. But Elena could see he was sad and distant.

[00:09:04] Elena: Porque él una noche llegó con un arma hechiza y ella decía que era corta y pega una arma de verdad, pero era de madera.

[00:09:16] Henry: Esteban showed up with a gun, or it looked like one but was really just a replica that was carved from wood. Still, his grandmother was worried, and she told Elena to be careful. By then the war had settled into a brutal tit-for-tat between the guerillas and the paramilitaries. Massacres had become commonplace in the area as the two battled for control of this lucrative drug staging area. Huge numbers of people had to flee. And young men like Esteban were being recruited regularly. Sometimes it was voluntary. Sometimes they were forced to join. It was around then that Elena went to the house and Esteban, his grandmother on his father’s side sat her down.

[00:09:57] Elena: Ya tiene varios días que él no duerme aquí en la casa.

[00:10:03] Henry: Esteban hadn’t slept in the house for days, the grandmother told her. They’d already started looking. Family. Friends. But no one had seen him. 

A few days later came a tip — someone had spotted him in another neighborhood.

[00:10:16] Elena: Me comentó que él había estado allá. Que él tenía un amigo que era un indio que era un peruano. Pero era indio. Y desaparecieron los dos.

[00:10:29] Henry: He’d been hanging out with an Indigenous man from Peru, the neighbor said. And one day the two of them just didn’t come back. 

But Elena had other questions. Did he run away? Did he join the guerrillas or the paramilitaries? Was he forced to join? What she did know was that she now had missing sons. So once again, she tried to follow every lead. She traveled to the neighborhood where Esteban was last seen and then walked the streets asking anyone who’d listen – have you seen a boy like this? 

But nothing. At the time, most people assumed Esteban had just run off. Same as Luis. And then in 2002 – a minor miracle happened.

[00:11:11] Elena: Pero un buen día apareció.

[00:11:15] Henry: Luis came back. 

Just like that. As inexplicably as he’d left. 

The full story remains unknown. But here’s what Elena could piece together. Luis was taken to Ecuador, where he eventually snuck away then ran for his life.

[00:11:30] Elena: Él dice que él se montó en una mula y cuando fue a ver, se fue. Estaba en el Ecuador.

[00:11:37] Henry: Eventually, he found a mule that got him across the border from Ecuador to Columbia where he made his way to Cali. One day, someone in the family heard a local radio station broadcasting messages of families who had lost their children or partners. They heard a voice calling for Luis. We can’t keep you, they told him, your family is looking for you. They gave him money, food and put him on the road back to Buenaventura. It was 2017. Years passed since Esteban disappeared. Elena lived in a kind of suspended animation. Searching. Waiting for him. And around here, Colombia was changing.

[00:12:29] Newswire: After more than five decades of bloodshed, there may be a chance for peace in Colombia again. The Colombian government and the Marxist guerrillas known as FARC, are due to sign a revised peace deal Thursday to end the conflict that has killed more than 100,000 people and forced millions more Colombians from their homes.

[00:12:48] Henry: Although in 2016 the Colombian government signed a peace deal with the FARC that ended more than five decades of war with the country’s biggest guerrilla organization, for Elena, the agreement brought hope, but not answers.

[00:13:01] Elena: Salimos muchas. Recuerdo que salimos alrededor de unas 111 personas.

[00:13:10] Henry: So, in 2017, about a hundred of them women who had lost children, husbands, wives, brothers, sisters, friends started meeting at a Catholic Church. It wasn’t really activism. It was like a support group. They were going to need each other.

[00:13:26] Newswire: La ola de violencia que vive el puerto tiene una razón. La disputa del territorio por parte de estas tres bandas delincuenciales. Todo por el control del narcotráfico.

[00:13:43] Henry: But the war wasn’t over. What came after the peace deal with the FARC was different. Smaller. Less ideological. More Criminal. And remarkably, more brutal. In addition to the remnants of the guerrillas and the paramilitaries, there were local gangs. Two of them ended up at war for control of Buenaventura. Fighting it out. Block by bloody block. And soon it reached Elena’s family. Again. This one, we were going to call him Josué. Now, he wasn’t actually Elena’s biological son. He was her nephew. But he and Esteban had grown up together in the same house raised like brothers.

[00:14:24] Elena: Era como un hijo para mí.

[00:14:25] Henry: Josué is like a son to me, she told us. Josué worked with his hands. He was a motorcycle mechanic. People said he could diagnose any engine just by looking at it. 

It was a Sunday in May 2021 when someone called him for a repair. He grabbed his tools and walked out of the door. He never came back. By Monday people in the neighborhood were saying Josué had been killed. It could have been one of the gangs or other armed groups in the area. Or it could’ve been a random crime. When war surrounds you, no one asks too many questions. At one point for example, someone had told her they had seen a young man from the area carrying his tools hiding them under his shirt. Sneaking into Josué’s room to grab his clothes. Who was he? Didn’t anyone stop him? Elaina still doesn’t know. 

She probably never will. Still, she looked. And this time with a sense of urgency, because Josué’s mom, Carmen, was dying. She felt like she had to get an answer about what happened to her son. She pushed organizations, she pushed authorities.

[00:15:39] Elena: Hay veces yo me iba todo el día a caminar con ella, a buscarlo.

[00:15:45] Henry: Carmen helped as well. Sometimes the two of them spent the whole day walking around looking. Months passed. Nothing. More months. And still nothing. And then, in December 2021. Something. A forensic team from the government had been searching all day in the estuaries that surrounded the city. The waterways are used for trafficking and dumping bodies. The team was finishing a sweep through them when the tide went out and they were beached. While they waited for the tide to return. Somebody looked towards the brush. There resting in the mud…

[00:16:29] Elena: Estaba el cráneo allí.

[00:16:41] Henry: …was a skull. Identifying the body was a painful process. It took years. Throughout, Elena had one concern.

[00:16:49] Elena: Yo no quiero que fallezca sin saber de su hijo.

[00:16:53] Henry: I don’t want Carmen to die without knowing what happened to her son, she told herself. Carmen died on August 14th, 2024. Thirteen days later, authorities declared the skull they had found was Josué’s. It had been three years since they had found it. It was so hard. Helena says she was the only one. Who looked when they showed them what remained of Josué.

[00:17:21] Elena: No le pudo dar el último adiós a su hijo. Uff… Dios bendito…uff…el dolor es inmenso.

[00:17:37] Henry: The pain is immense. Three Children. Three Searches. 

Luis left, and Luis came back. Josué was killed. Elena buried him. And Esteban?

[00:17:46] Elena: Y así estoy yo hoy. Esperando. Esperando que mi hijo aparezca.

[00:17:53] Henry: Elena is still waiting.

[00:17:57] Elena: Aunque sea un huesito. Aunque sea un huesito de la mano, del pie, de alguna parte del cuerpo que aparezca y le digan a uno: es mi hijo.

[00:18:09] Henry: Even a small bone she says, from his and his foot anywhere. So someone could finally tell her: this, this is your son.

[00:18:36] Steven Dudley: This show is a production of InSight Crime. Before we go a quick look at next week.

[00:18:41] Rapper: La droga que sale de aquí porque sale.

[00:18:44] Steven Dudley: We met him in Ecuador. He’s a rapper. On stage, he’s got the microphone. Off-stage, something else entirely. It’s a story about music and crime, and the line between them. You won’t want to miss this one.

Now, about the episode you just heard. It was reported and written by Henry Shuldiner and Juliana Manjarrés. Edited by Liza Schmidt, Tomás Uprimny, Elisa Roldán and me, Steven Dudley. Context: Buenaventura, Colombia’s Armed Conflict and Criminal Violence

Buenaventura, Colombia, concentrates some of the country’s starkest contradictions. It is Colombia’s most important Pacific port and handles around 60% of the country’s foreign trade. At the same time, it is one of the cities with the highest levels of poverty, unemployment, and violence in the country.

Its geographic position has made it a key hub for drug trafficking: it sits next to Colombia’s largest coca-producing region and has direct access to maritime routes toward Europe and North America. Its strategic importance first attracted the rebels of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Fuerzas Revolucionarias de Colombia – FARC), then their bitter enemies in counterinsurgency groups.

Both the paramilitaries and the FARC have demobilized following peace accords, but in both cases the power vacuum was filled by successor groups and local gangs.

Today, two groups in particular—the Espartanos and the Shottas—fight a neighborhood-by-neighborhood war for control of the city’s strategic corridors, generating waves of forced displacement and disappearances that disproportionately affected people in low-income neighborhoods.

Forced disappearances in Buenaventura have a particular characteristic: many bodies are thrown into estuaries—the waterways surrounding the city—making the identification of remains extremely difficult and prolonging families’ suffering indefinitely. Victims’ organizations have spent decades demanding a stronger response from the Colombian state.

headline: Elections and Organized Crime
article_body:
Organized crime has long played a role in elections across Latin America and the Caribbean, from financing  political campaigns to influencing local governance, voter participation, and state institutions through corruption, coercion, and violence. Tracking and understanding these dynamics is critical to explaining how criminal groups build political capital and how democratic institutions are weakened over time.

The Latest: Peru Elections 2026

Peru’s presidential run-off remains too close to call, with conservative Keiko Fujimori and leftist Roberto Sánchez Palomino locked in a technical tie as of June 8 and vote counting expected to continue for days—or even weeks.

The election pits two starkly different visions for the country against one another. Fujimori, making her fourth bid for the presidency, has promised a tough-on-crime crackdown inspired by the hardline policies of her father, former president Alberto Fujimori. Sánchez Palomino has focused more heavily on social inequality and institutional reform, while also pledging to address growing insecurity.

Many Peruvians hope the eventual winner can halt a cycle of political instability that has seen the country go through eight presidents in a decade, while organized crime has expanded across the country. Extortion, illegal mining, and corruption have all flourished amid years of political turmoil and weakened state institutions.

The deadlocked result suggests Peru’s political turmoil may be far from over, raising fresh questions about the next government’s ability to confront the country’s mounting security challenges.

Check back soon for InSight Crime’s analysis of Peru’s elections and the criminal threats facing the country’s next president.

For the last 15 years, InSight Crime has covered the relationship between organized crime and politics across the Americas. In Guatemala, we have measured political risk and mapped the corruption and power networks that have shaped recent election cycles. We have also reported on how organized crime groups in Mexico and pro-government armed groups  in Venezuela have used violence and intimidation to influence voting and maintain political control.

What can Washington’s new “cartel coalition” deliver? 

What does the arrest of CJNG operators in Europe say about the group’s resilience?

And can a joint police push stop Brazil’s two biggest gangs from carving up Bolivia’s border with Brazil?

This week’s top three organized crime stories in On the Radar.

1. ‘Shield of the Americas’ Meets in Panama

The Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (A3C), the 17-nation bloc launched by the Trump administration, met in Panama City this week to begin planning joint action against drug trafficking and organized crime. US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth arrived Wednesday to deliver remarks at the forum, and the gathering took place as the Pentagon retired Joint Task Force-Southern Spear, the operation behind the lethal boat strikes that have killed more than 220 people over the last year.

There are questions about what A3C can actually deliver. The coalition is largely a bloc of right-leaning governments keen to align with Trump’s strategy, the latest addition being Colombia under its new president, Abelardo de la Espriella. But Brazil and Mexico—two countries central to the region’s drug trade—are absent. The A3C’s founding declaration includes only four points, with no long-term commitments on burden-sharing among member states and no proposals for tracking cross-border criminal flows or investigating government corruption. Instead, the framework leans heavily on militarized enforcement, ignoring the drivers that sustain organized crime: weak judicial systems, poor governance, and the poverty that keeps illicit economies profitable. 

InSight Crime’s investigation into what the firepower behind Southern Spear has actually achieved found little evidence the strikes have dented cocaine flows, even as the death toll and price tag have climbed—a pattern that A3C’s militarized focus risks repeating.

2. CJNG Operators Charged Over Guns-for-Drugs Deal in Czech Republic

The US Justice Department this week unsealed an indictment against four alleged members of the Jalisco Cartel New Generation (Cartel Jalisco Nueva Generación – CJNG) for allegedly negotiating a deal to trade fentanyl and methamphetamine for European machine guns, rocket-propelled grenade launchers, and mortars. Two of the men were extradited and appeared in court this week; the other two await extradition. Prosecutors describe the network’s alleged financier as the godson of captured CJNG regional commander Audias Flores Silva, alias “El Jardinero.”

The case underscores how the CJNG’s international reach now extends well beyond drug trafficking and into arms procurement in Europe—even as the group’s leadership structure keeps absorbing hits from Mexican and US authorities. But removing a leader or mid-level operator rarely shuts a group down; more often it fractures it into smaller factions that compete violently for territory and don’t answer to any central command. The CJNG’s leadership structure has already been reshuffled repeatedly this year, yet the group’s drug and arms trafficking operations continue.

3. Bolivia and Brazil Launch Joint Border Push as PCC and Red Command Fight for Territory

Bolivia and Brazil are set to launch a binational security plan, Secure Borders (Fronteras Seguras), on Thursday in the border town of Guayaramerín, following a deadly turf war thought to be between Brazil’s two largest criminal organizations. Bolivian authorities have already deployed more than 300 police to the region after a wave of killings they blame on Brazil’s Red Command (Comando Vermelho – CV) and the First Capital Command (Primeiro Comando da Capital – PCC), which they say are fighting over a cocaine export corridor.

Bolivia’s emergence as a battleground reflects a broader shift: the PCC and Red Command have been steadily moving their regional operations out of Paraguay and into Bolivia, drawn by its proximity to coca-growing regions and its more than 3,400-kilometer border with Brazil. A binational police plan may slow the violence but does not address why Bolivia’s borders have become so attractive to Brazil’s gangs in the first place: the area is difficult to patrol, corruption is rampant, and until recently, there was no Drug Enforcement Administration presence in the country.
